A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MAVFusion work, and their text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison. V1 includes Appendices A–C; v2 ends at the references. Appendix results incorporated into v2's main text were matched before identifying removals.

before.justification: V1 reports original fusion benchmarks, ablations, efficiency measurements, detection and segmentation examples, and image-dataset robustness experiments in Section 4 and Appendices A–C.

after.justification: V2 retains original fusion benchmarks, ablations, efficiency measurements and downstream detection results in Section 4, Tables 1–3 and Figures 4–7.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 revises the specified attention operation from one background token averaged across patches to N individually pooled patch tokens supplying keys and values. This is a localized revision to the documented procedure; the overall architecture and losses remain. The PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed.

E1.justification: V2 removes the MSRS, LLVIP and M3FD image-fusion evaluations and the SAMWISE pedestrian video-segmentation task from Appendices B–C. This substantially narrows task and input-condition coverage. Fusion on M3SVD, HDO and VTMOT and downstream object detection remain.

E2.justification: MaskDiFuser and TemCoCo are removed from the fusion and detection comparisons. VideoFusion's existing appendix comparisons move into the main text, while VideoFusion newly joins the efficiency comparison in Table 3. Most comparator membership is retained.

E3.justification: Removed evaluation procedures include SAMWISE segmentation at t and t+2 and applying video-trained weights to nonsequential images without retraining. The retained experiments keep the same five-sequence test splits, metrics, training settings and efficiency-test resolutions. Newly specifying the Top-K ratio does not establish a changed setting.

E4.justification: V2 removes Appendix C's experiment presented as testing robustness to unreliable optical flow, eliminating a substantive examination of dependence on motion cues. Appendix B's segmentation error case studies also disappear. The region-separation, sparse-attention and MAFM ablations in Table 2 remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates or statistical significance tests for the experimental results. Uncertainty-reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: V2 removes MaskDiFuser and TemCoCo results, all three image-dataset result blocks and segmentation findings. Table 3 adds VideoFusion efficiency measurements, including 7.83 and 2.59 FPS at 640×480 and 1280×720. Common benchmark, ablation and efficiency values remain unchanged; VideoFusion's fusion scores match v1 Table 4.

T1.justification: Equation 6 substantively changes the mathematical definition of global context from an across-patch average to a set of per-patch pooled tokens. The accompanying explanation makes the k-query, N-key construction consistent with the stated O(kN) attention complexity. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims about motion-aware alignment, static–dynamic separation, sparse interaction, fusion quality and efficiency. The abstract's reported 14.16 FPS and the conclusion's three-benchmark performance claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 4.7 replaces the specific limitation of optical-flow errors corrupting motion masks with difficulty extracting reliable features under severe degradation. Appendix C's explanation that Top-K selection and the static branch compensate for unreliable flow is removed. Ablation and efficiency prose also qualifies previously imprecise performance statements.

D1.justification: V2 discloses a Top-K retention ratio of 0.3 and explains that temporal weights start at one, undergo temporal Softmax normalization and are optimized end-to-end. It clarifies flow directions and changes the code-access statement from forthcoming to available. Hardware and main training details remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds Xian et al.'s work on shared representations and removes references to SAMWISE, TemCoCo, LLVIP, PIAFusion and Mask-DiFuser. Related-work examples are shortened, but the main positioning is retained. Publication updates for retained works, including VideoFusion, do not constitute new cited research.

P1.justification: The main section order remains intact, with localized condensation and rewriting in the introduction, related work, methodology and experimental discussion. Acknowledgments expand. Appendix A is partly consolidated into the main experiments, while the remaining appendix sections are removed.

P2.justification: Experimental displays are substantially consolidated: VideoFusion panels from Figures 8–9 and rows from Table 4 enter Figures 4–7 and Table 1, replacing MaskDiFuser displays. TemCoCo displays, segmentation Figure 10 and image-benchmark Table 5 disappear. Figure 2 redraws the MAFM residual path, and Table 3 gains an efficiency row.

improvement.justification: V2 improves mathematical consistency and implementation disclosure and adds a useful VideoFusion efficiency comparison. However, removing robustness and segmentation evidence, evaluated comparators and the specific flow-mask failure caveat weakens empirical coverage and transparency. The removed TemCoCo comparison includes better HDO MS2R than MAVFusion, 0.9294 versus 0.9826 (v1 Table 4; lower is better). The principal experiments remain intact, making this a limited net deterioration.
